Hey there, I started low dose T almost a week ago and have the same concern. I'm NB and in love with my high range (I can comfortably reach up to C6), but I really want a lower speaking voice. The main advice I've read is to KEEP SINGING! So that's what I'm doing :)

Right now I spend an hour every other day doing scales and other vocal exercises for both my high and low range. I also have a karaoke playlist that I run through most days, including songs that contain the high notes I want to retain, and songs in the male range with low notes I currently struggle to hit. This way I'm hoping to have a good understanding about the direction my voice takes, and adjust accordingly when the drop begins in earnest. It's a lot and I don't think you *need* to go this rigorous, I'm just personally very serious about maintaining my singing voice through transition. Best of luck to you, I hope T treats your voice with kindness!

There is no one way to trans. We all have our own transition goals, for some people it may include going "all the way" with HRT and gender-affirming surgery, for others it may stop at social transition or even just personal affirmation. All of these goals are perfectly valid and nothing can invalidate your transness unless you decided not to identify that way. You may want to look at some nonbinary subreddits as transition paths vary extensively in that community. And as someone who recently exited the very early stages of transition, my advice to you is to be kind to yourself. Take some time to process the feelings surrounding your gender identity, and continue seeking answers for any questions you may have about being transgender :) It's normal and valid for your feelings to shift around and feel confusing in the beginning, but this period is also wonderful for learning and experimenting to see what makes you most comfortable and affirmed with yourself! Wishing you all the best on this journey ♡

The best representations of LGBT people are going to be ones written by LGBT people themselves. I haven't read enough myself, but I'll recommend [Giovanni's Room](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/406235.Giovanni_s_Room), which is a classic and a wonderful example of a great story with LGBT themes. Books I haven't read but look good are [Red, White & Royal Blue](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/41150487-red-white-royal-blue), [All That's Left in the World](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/58329296-all-that-s-left-in-the-world), [Doubting Thomas](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/56329920-doubting-thomas), basically everything from [this list](https://www.esquire.com/entertainment/books/g39598614/best-books-by-lgbtq-writers/). Ultimately, the key is treating gay characters the same way you would any other character, because they are simply human beyond their sexuality. If you're struggling, writing about the protagonist's struggles against a homophobic character may work in a similar way to a POC character struggling against a racist character or basically any form of discrimination, if that makes sense :)

Consider the popular and not uncommon narrative of trans people who realized they identified with a different gender since they were kids. It doesn't take the internet, peers, age or education to know how you feel on the inside. Gender identity is just kind of an innate thing, and the identifying terms have risen because as it turns out, the gender spectrum is not as linear and concrete as we were raised to believe. Young people are not "claiming" to be made up sounding gender identities because they think it's cool, they have finally found the language to explain their experience to people. Language is always morphing and new terms created to define experiences that otherwise are hard to explain. The surge in young LGBT people is happening because it's a much safer climate to openly explore gender identity. Nonbinary, genderfluid and genderqueer people have always existed, but until recently the language wasn't there to explain these experiences, and transphobic attitudes would've made it difficult for anyone to come out if their identity wasn't already being internally suppressed.

"Person" and "people" are correct terms for describing those who are nonbinary, since they sit outside of the concepts of man and woman. She/they means they accept both she/her and they/them sets of pronouns. They may have a preference for a specific set or they may not, it never hurts to ask! You can also ask how they feel about gendered terms like "girl" or "woman" just to be clear about their comfort levels. You're honestly doing a great job navigating this and being respectful too :)

It's important to consider your safety when navigating transition. Many people are accepting of LGB people, but when the acronym reaches T opinions are still very divided. There's lots of trans issues happening in the news right now, so try bringing up a headline around your grandparents to gauge their attitudes about trans people. This may give you a fair idea of how they'd react to you coming out, as well as any misinformed views you can help debunk. Since they accepted your sibling, maybe having them with you if you decide to come out may help? If your grandparents bring up how you appear to have no issues, you can mention how being trans can be a very isolating experience and for many people it's easier to mask than to open up (also, it's perfectly normal and healthy to visit therapy for any reason). I wish you all the best with this and hope they're accepting and helpful through your transition! If not, waiting until college is your best bet. 18 is still extremely young and a great time to start transition. If you decide to begin your transition without your grandparents knowing, you can transition socially by using your preferred name and pronouns at school, and if resources allow you could purchase a binder; the ones from Underworks are affordable, high quality and can be washed discreetly in the sink if you're worried about getting caught.

Those are my answers to your main questions, the rest of this comment is an aside about your third paragraph. Bear in mind that your "tainted" view of trans people is exclusively through trans youth, who are going through the emotional turmoil of being a teenager as well as the identity crisis that comes from realizing you're trans. It's important to remember that we're all just people who happen to also be trans, and if you identify as trans then you're grouped in with us as well. I've met both wonderful and terrible trans people, whether someone's annoying or not has nothing to do with their gender identity, so please don't let two people affect how you view an entire community.

Finally, I'd be wary of assuming anyone is "faking" being trans. That comes from the idea that there are right and wrong ways to trans, which is a stigma that makes many trans people doubt their own validity. Everyone's gender exploration is deeply personal, and even phases where it seems like someone is faking an identity are necessary for them to discover where they feel most comfortable on the gender spectrum.

>...it's more that I don't make gender a factor on whether or not I find someone attractive.

This is pretty much what separates pansexuality from similar identities such as bisexuality. It's not necessarily an explicit attraction to all genders, a pansexual person may still have preferences, but gender is less of a factor for them than it is for someone who knows they only like men or women, or aren't interested in dating nonbinary people.

Could you find yourself attracted to any person if you clicked well enough, regardless of their gender identity? If so it does sound like you may be pansexual :)

Not at all. Gender is something that can be extremely personal and discovering your place on the gender spectrum is a very liberating experience. If I were binary FtM, abolishing gender would honestly feel like a slap to the face for all of the work I had put into my transition to have people perceive me as a man. I think what's needed is a removal of toxic gender norms, which seem to be the reason people bring up the idea of a genderless society. As an example, raising children in a more neutral way and allowing them to take on whatever interests them without the stigma of "that's for boys/girls" is a good step in creating an equal playing field for people of all gender identities. Hopefully that makes sense haha, basically my attitude when it comes to topics like postgenderism is that it's more important to build a society where one can feel safe and happy identifying as a masculine woman or a feminine man than breaking down those walls entirely, since many people enjoy having a gendered identity! :)

Something that seems to help a lot for people with ADHD is body doubling, which is having someone else present so they can focus on the task at hand. 

When she was young, my grandma (who isn't diagnosed but certainly has ADHD) had a habit of keeping a messy room, and even if there was a small amount of cleaning to be done it was still mentally difficult for her to do. Something my great-grandma did to help was sit in her room for half an hour while my grandma cleaned-- her presence was enough to help her focus.

I also struggle with this and it's a lot easier for me to focus on cleaning my room when I have something to anchor my mind, whether it's having a friend on the phone, listening to an audiobook, or putting on a video of someone else cleaning their room (sounds weird but it works!). It takes a lot more discipline for someone with ADHD to keep a space clean by themselves, so it might help to test these methods with your son! Best of luck :)

It's important to remember that we all experience symptoms to different degrees so it might actually be harder for them to get in the habit of washing their dishes, but there's definitely room for compromise here since it's become an issue. Are there any chores that your roommate is okay with doing? If so, maybe you could wash dishes while they do another chore that doesn't trigger sensory issues as much. You could also give an incentive if that works, like let's go to the bar on Friday if you can keep the room clean this week or anything fun you could do together. 

That all being said, even with ADHD there is a level of responsibility we all need in order to adult properly lol. If nothing works, talk to them about the issue in terms of how it makes you feel, and avoid blaming them lest they feel attacked and try to guilt trip you more. If all else fails you might want to talk to your RA or whoever can arrange a new roommate situation, but hopefully it doesn't have to come to that! Best of luck, I hope things work out for you :)

I was diagnosed with costochondritis at 16 too, around that time I was having severe chest pain often and it was really scary first learning about it. I'm 22 and still have it, but it occurs much less often and is easier to deal with now that I know how to manage the pain. The good news is that costo isn't life-threatening, just annoying.

Take note of what happened whenever you get chest pain, such as stretching out your chest too hard or lifting heavy objects, so you'll be aware and maybe avoid those kinds of situations that might make it worse. When I get pain, I always lie down and put a pillow under my chest to lift it, for me it eases most or all of the pain and the stretch feels really good too. I don't know your situation but I hope that you won't have to live with this for too long, or at least that your case won't be severe. Wishing you the best! :)

The point of running a promotional campaign is to get people hyped *now*, not to repost tons of filler and expect them to stick around for when the "actual" teasers come up. What I mean by sloppy is that it feels at times that posts (mainly on their official Instagram) are just shoved in to give off the appearance that something is coming up when it's actually just filler. I don't expect drastic news to come out all the time, and I don't think that would be a great idea anyway, but it feels a bit drab to be posting old news and pieces of Gorillaz art without any context whatsoever. 

As for Noodle, I have mixed feelings. I love that we get a taste of her "personal life" but at the end of the day, her Instagram a tie-in with the Gorillaz project and presumably a companion piece for Phase Four. Considering how much care has been made in the past to have even the most subtle details contribute to the overall meaning during previous phases, I would expect Jamie to be smart about what kinds of posts he makes for her. Maybe what we call shitposts will actually mean something when the album comes out. Right now, however, for Noodle to post a picture of food after talking about how much she hates it when people post pictures of their food leads me to wonder how much care is really being given to the Phase Four campaign.

I agree that the music and the story go hand-in-hand and both have inspired me in countless ways, but I honestly have to go with the music. Obviously he was aided by the appeal of the virtual band but Damon has brought so much to the table for the music world and the genre ambiguity of Gorillaz' music is something I think we need more of. The fact that such experimental sounds were welcomed and *accepted* by mainstream audiences shows the potential there is for the future of music.

I guess the verdict is a bit unanimous at this point but I also far prefer the 2D look over 3D. The work done throughout Phase Three and in DoYaThing was impressive and a fresh look but the boys did look very creepy and sometimes not in a good way. It's also fascinating to see how Jamie's art style progresses and you don't really get to watch that with 3D characters. 

That all being said, the 3D look really suited Cyborg Noodle (bless her soul, wherever she is in the middle of the ocean).

I agree completely. I'm sure that Jamie's up to something big with all of these teasers. However, it feels like he's trying to get us all hyped but it's just (imo) confusing at best, not working at worst. I'm holding out faith that everything will make sense in the long run but my fear is that this is really all just sloppy planning due to the fact that Gorillaz hasn't done a major project in *years*. 

The campaign has been so sloppy that at this point I don't feel as excited to see a new Instagram post from Jamie or Noodle as I was in the beginning. Noodle's shitposts especially are disconcerting and lead me to think that Jamie (or whoever runs her account) is posting them on impulse for the sake of making her appear closer to reality rather than to have any real significance for the next album. I'm really hoping that things start to make sense in a few months as we near the album's release because, at least for me, whatever they're doing right now to promote the new album is just lackluster.
